It wants nothing but itself, to enjoy itself.
These <…> are kitsch formulations left behind by former theologians.
“In German, one lies whenever one is polite.”
In German, politeness turns too quickly into irony.
What is missing is the self-aware play of convention.
The slyness of a journeyman’s language corrupted by theologians.
The reservation of inwardness. For a hundred years now, since positivism, it has been malicious.
Its true poet is Wilhelm Busch: the humorist of malicious pleasure and envy.
When I read what Edmund A. Walsh had written about me and my Concept of the Political in True Rather Than False Geopolitics for Germany (1946), the word Schafsnase escaped my lips.
That is how deeply I remain trapped in a purely intellectual attitude.
Even toward someone already swinging the noose with which he intends to put it around my neck.

Only afterward did it occur to me that this passage was an act of nastiness deliberately calculated for Schafsnasen. And that this nastiness in turn goes back to a crook, poor Gurian, who in his own way is trying to avenge himself for his own crookedness and uses a Jesuit to do it.
Here we see the chain of purposes and motives.
Chains and webs like this are what appear to us poor human beings when we try to understand the “connections” through which God’s providence supposedly “works.”
But God does not work. Only the crooks work.
So let them carry on working.
God had long since turned everything toward the good by the time [they] pulled the trigger and set their tools and projectiles in motion.
A boundary has something magical about it.
Spatially magical. So says R. Kassner.
In time, what corresponds to the boundary is not another boundary but the “turn,” the moment of change.
Time corresponds not to magic but to freedom.
Tone, rather than word and myth.

With boyish seriousness, as an “ancient” man, I concern myself with the magic of space. I do not want to grasp it. Still less do I want to manufacture it. But I want to know it, and by knowing it preserve it for others.
I see the final space: my grave. I see it dissolving.
My homeland, the river—everything is being destroyed. But I hold on to it.
And they go down with me.
The secret of my life. This is my property. I take it with me into the grave.

Property is only what one can take into the grave. So today there is no property left. Only the dead body. And that, apparently, is better burned. So the pacifists, the abortionists, and the advocates of cremation triumph.
After reading Kant, Kleist told a friend: now there is nothing left that one can take into the grave.
Hegel: the Holy Sepulchre is empty.
The error of the Crusades. That is how they—and Däubler—interpret the resurrection of the flesh.
The only thing I inherit is my own body.
Däubler: thinghood is dead; the word fills space!
Däubler’s Northern Lights is not word. It is tone. It is tonality.
Every act of destruction necessarily produces so many attempts at restoration that the confusion becomes terrible.
Typical of the rubbish bin attached to every modern movement: all the anti-alcohol people; the anti-nicotine people; the anti-meat people; all the Bible Students; everyone joins in.
Naturally, the fellow-traveller is the only person who is truly guilty.
Making the sign of the cross produces greater world-spanning radiation than all the manufacturers of atomic bombs.
I make the sign of the cross over the chaos of my affects and emotions.
With Annette, the sign of the cross becomes only the “phosphorus plant,” the plant of life.
Her tribute to her age. She paid it with feminine humility and honesty.
Equally deep and honest is her service in the “temple,” as she calls it. But why does she say “temple”? She is not ancient at all. There is nothing humanist or classical about her.
Meanwhile even Max Stirner, with his nihilism, has become nothing more than a boaster. He once seemed so irrefutably right.
What could be more immediate, more inalienable, more undeniable than my body and my ownership of it?
Surely I take it into the grave with me?
You do not take it into the grave. It goes into the crematorium.
Perhaps its ashes will be scattered to every wind.
Brother Straubinger practised this with a bad conscience. Those who followed as victors appear to have practised it with a good one.
Which is worse here: the good conscience or the bad?
A good conscience organized with the help of the justice system is the worst thing of all.
“The others did evil things with a good conscience; we do good things with a bad one.”
That is the situation which, both inwardly and outwardly, attracts every demon of revenge and every plunderer.
The vis attractiva of the bad conscience: its power of attraction.
Twice as powerful in the case of a fundamentally stupid and wretched devil whom German cultivated culture first summoned into existence and then abandoned.
The World Spirit grants absolution to the good conscience of those who are completely evil.

Naturally, anyone who has the opportunity to legalize his power simply by declaring it to be law will make use of that wonderful opportunity. He will not allow this <…> legal <…> surplus value to escape him.
No ruler has ever given up such an opportunity. This too belongs to the total phenomenon of legal “positivism” in the age of legality.
I take nothing into the grave. Because the graves themselves are being destroyed, even if I still manage to reach my own private grave.
Today property is only what one takes into death.
Germany: put in brackets and at the same time bracketed out, inside a world splitting open.
Now these intellectuals abuse the poor German people and list all its faults and disgraces.
The model is Luther abusing the poor peasants. Or the Anabaptists in 1535.
German cultivated culture itself shares in the guilt. It seems unable to escape this pattern.
The reverse case is fundamentally the same:
Goethe’s heroic poem about old Blücher—“conscious and great”!

Measured by the standards that rule today, Kierkegaard was a dreadful reactionary and enemy of the people. He would have to be discriminated against, defamed, dismantled, and exterminated. And that is without even mentioning D.[onoso] C.[ortés].
My mistake was the good-naturedness of my attempts to adapt.
My inability to believe that human beings could really be as stupid and vulgar as they are, and as they prove to me every day.

It would be instructive—and necessary—to make a sociological comparison between the émigrés who returned to France in 1815 and those who returned to Germany in 1945. But even as a passing observation, that is probably already life-threatening and blasphemous.

“La Petite Cité”—the “Little City,” as distinct from the Grande Cité—the inner circle: this is what Augustin Cochin calls the specific formation for which I am trying to find a name: elite, political-criminal association, and so on. What matters is that he got his inspiration from Bryce and Ostrogorski—that is, from the “machine” of a political “party.” O Roberto Michels, come to our aid! “Petite Cité” is not good. But matière votante—“voting material”—is magnificent.

Again and again Cochin stresses the “social forces”: ces êtres inhumains, un Chalier, un Marat, un Carrier ne sont que les produits mécaniques du travail collectif—these inhuman beings, a Chalier, a Marat, a Carrier, are merely the mechanical products of collective activity. Calling it anarchy—or nihilism—explains nothing. Those are merely the rotting entrails from which, according to Aristotle, bees are born.
Do you now understand the full enormity of my crime? It is one of those crimes that can never be forgiven: curiosity about the true motives and the real driving forces behind organized indignation.
Augustin Cochin, Sociétés de pensée, p. 111: “The thesis of self-defense appears with democracy itself.”
